Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
Being in a situation where someone has power over me

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
make sure to stay close to exit

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I have to be on guard all the time

issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile, 'kids crying' is not impossible, but it is a relatively specific trigger that would usually be supported by memory or appraisal content involving civilians/children; here the memory and appraisal items do not provide that link, so this trigger is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' implies an enduring physical injury theme, but the rest of the selected items do not support a bodily injury-focused combat presentation: memory items emphasize fragmentation/unreality, triggers emphasize intrusion/power imbalance, and strategies emphasize avoidance/hypervigilance rather than injury management. This appraisal is insufficiently anchored in the rest of the profile.

vignette: Leilani's eyes still scan the horizon, even after all these years. It's a habit she formed during her tour in Afghanistan, where every sound and movement held potential danger. Now, at 66, she finds herself doing it automatically, often without realizing it. But some sounds still bring it all flooding back - the whir of helicopter blades, for instance. When she hears that, Leilani is instantly transported to a dusty Afghan village, reliving a day that has become etched in her memory like a scar. That day, Leilani's unit was ambushed by insurgents while on patrol. She remembers the chaos and confusion, the feeling of being completely at the mercy of others as she scrambled for cover behind a crumbling wall. The power imbalance was stark - they had guns, explosives, and the upper hand; her team had training, but that day it wasn't enough. Even now, Leilani can feel the weight of that helplessness settling on her like a physical force. After leaving the military, Leilani tried to build a new life as a curriculum designer. She enjoyed shaping young minds and creating engaging lesson plans, but the memories lingered, fragmented and disjointed. Some days, she'd catch herself staring blankly at a spreadsheet or textbook, unable to recall what she was doing there. The story of that ambush still feels unreal, like something from a movie - which makes it all the more difficult for Leilani to put into words. When people ask about her time in combat, she freezes, struggling to find the right phrases. To cope, Leilani has developed some strategies over the years. She avoids going out unless absolutely necessary; social gatherings feel like minefields, and the thought of being trapped in a crowded room with no clear exit route sends her anxiety spiking. When emotions threaten to overwhelm her, she pushes them down, unwilling to let herself be swayed by feelings that might cloud her judgment. And always - always - she positions herself near an exit, whether it's at work or at home. Despite these efforts, Leilani can't shake the feeling of being on guard all the time. She questions every decision, no matter how small, and fears making mistakes that could put others in harm's way. At night, she lies awake, replaying the what-ifs of that ambush, wondering if there was something - anything - she could have done differently. The self-doubt eats away at her like a slow-moving acid. Leilani feels isolated, disconnected from those around her who can't possibly understand what she's been through. Her ex-husband tried to be supportive, but eventually gave up; the distance between them grew until it became too wide to bridge. Now, Leilani's social circle is shrinking, comprised mainly of acquaintances and colleagues who don't press for details. Recently, a new project at work required her to create educational materials about conflict resolution. As she delved deeper into the subject matter, the memories began to resurface with renewed intensity. Leilani found herself avoiding meetings, skipping team lunches, and procrastinating on deadlines - all attempts to keep the feelings of powerlessness and panic at bay. One morning, as she was working from home, a helicopter flew low overhead, its rotors thundering through the air. The sound sent Leilani crashing back into that Afghan village, heart racing and palms slick with sweat. In that moment, she realized she couldn't keep living like this - perpetually on edge, constantly retreating from life itself. With a newfound determination, Leilani made an appointment to see a therapist, hoping to confront the memories head-on and learn how to quiet the constant din of hypervigilance in her mind.
